::: {.section-card}

This report provides a data-driven assessment of skills demand and training
supply in Poland, with a particular focus on the extent to which publicly
visible training provision is aligned with employers' needs. The analysis
combines two large-scale sources of labour-market intelligence: online job
postings from
<a class="paper-link" href="https://www.pracuj.pl/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Pracuj.pl</a>,
used as a proxy for employer demand, and training-service listings from
<a class="paper-link" href="https://uslugirozwojowe.parp.gov.pl/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Baza Usług Rozwojowych (BUR)</a>,
used as a proxy for the supply of structured upskilling and reskilling
opportunities. By applying natural language processing methods to both
datasets, the report translates unstructured vacancy and training descriptions
into comparable skill categories.

The central objective of the report is not to estimate the total number of
jobs or training participants in Poland, but to compare the composition of
skills demanded by employers with the composition of skills offered through
the training system. This distinction is important. Online vacancies capture
a specific segment of labour demand, especially market-based and
private-sector recruitment, while BUR reflects the supply of registered
training services rather than actual enrolment or completion. Despite these
limitations, both sources provide timely and granular evidence that can
complement official labour-market statistics and support more responsive
skills policies.

The report is organised around three analytical questions. First, what types
of skills are currently demanded in the Polish labour market, and how does
this demand vary across sectors and regions? Second, what skills are being
supplied through BUR training services, and how has this provision evolved
over time? Third, where are the main mismatches between employer demand and
training supply, especially in areas that are strategically relevant for
productivity, inclusion, and structural transformation?

A key contribution of the analysis is the use of standardised skill
taxonomies, primarily ESCO, to make job-posting and training data comparable.
This enables the report to move beyond broad occupational categories and
examine the specific competences, knowledge fields, and transversal skills
that appear in both demand and supply. Additional analysis focuses on
selected policy-relevant domains, including digital skills, artificial
intelligence, green skills, care-related work, public health training, and
job opportunities explicitly open to Ukrainian workers.

The findings show that Poland's skill ecosystem is characterised by both
strengths and gaps. Employer demand is strongly oriented toward management,
communication, collaboration, digital, ICT, and business-related skills.
Training supply, by contrast, places relatively greater emphasis on care,
services, health, welfare, and machinery-related skills. This does not imply
that these areas are overfunded or unimportant; many are linked to major
demographic and social challenges. However, it does suggest that the current
training portfolio may not fully reflect the structure of market-based
employer demand, particularly in areas linked to digitalisation,
organisational capabilities, and productivity growth.

The report also highlights the importance of interpreting data sources
carefully. Pracuj.pl vacancies provide rich and timely information on
employer demand, but they underrepresent some public-sector, informal,
low-wage, and locally recruited jobs. BUR data offer valuable insights into
training provision, but they do not measure training quality, take-up,
completion, or labour-market outcomes. Therefore, the results should be read
as evidence on the structure and direction of demand and supply, rather than
as a definitive measure of aggregate labour-market shortages.

For policymakers, the report points to the value of building an integrated
labour-market intelligence system that combines online vacancy data, training
registries, administrative sources, and standardised skills taxonomies. Such
a system could help identify emerging skill needs earlier, monitor whether
training provision is adapting to structural change, and guide public
investment in skills toward areas with the highest economic and social
returns. In the Polish context, this is particularly relevant for digital
transformation, the green transition, demographic ageing, migrant
integration, and regional development.

:::
